target.title: fix(agents): skip bootstrap seeding in inherited nested workspaces (#83593)
target.body:
## Summary

`ensureAgentWorkspace` re-seeds bootstrap templates (`SOUL.md`, `USER.md`, `IDENTITY.md`, `HEARTBEAT.md`, …) into directories nested **inside** an already-established OpenClaw workspace, because it only consulted the directory's *own* `.openclaw/workspace-state.json` marker — never an ancestor's. As reported in #83593, spawning a subagent (or starting a session in a nested git worktree) recreates bootstrap files the user intentionally relocated under the real workspace root, littering the parent workspace.

`resolveAgentWorkspaceDir` legitimately places secondary-agent workspaces at `path.join(agents.defaults.workspace, agentId)` — i.e. *inside* the established workspace — which is the structural root of the bug.

### Fix

Before seeding, skip only when the directory (a) is nested under an **ancestor** workspace marker, (b) does **not** own a workspace marker of its own, and (c) already holds non-trivial content (`hasSkipBootstrapWorkspaceContentEvidence`). That precisely targets inherited project content — a nested git worktree or relocated files.

- A directory that **owns** its `.openclaw/workspace-state.json` (a real secondary-agent workspace) keeps the normal seeding/repair path, so a required file removed after setup is still restored.
- An **empty** directory still seeds, so a freshly created secondary agent under `agents.defaults.workspace` keeps its starter files.
- Real workspace **roots** have no ancestor marker and are unaffected.

This matches the maintainer review's "narrow workspace-boundary fix … preserving documented starter-file creation for real workspace roots and required setup files," and avoids the two earlier closed attempts' pitfalls — no broad `isBrandNewWorkspace` gate, no hardcoded subdir names.

### Changes

- `src/agents/workspace.ts`: add `hasAncestorWorkspaceMarker(dir)` (walks ancestors for `.openclaw/workspace-state.json`); add the seeding guard in `ensureAgentWorkspace` (ancestor marker + no own marker + existing content).
- `src/agents/workspace.test.ts`: three regression tests — inherited content under a marker is **not** re-seeded; a brand-new nested secondary-agent dir **still** seeds; a nested workspace that **owns** its marker still repairs a missing required file under an ancestor marker.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: a subagent/session run recreates bootstrap files (`SOUL.md`, `USER.md`, `IDENTITY.md`, `HEARTBEAT.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `TOOLS.md`) inside a directory nested under an already-established OpenClaw workspace (#83593).
- Real environment tested: macOS (Darwin 25.x), Node 22, driving the real exported `ensureAgentWorkspace` from `src/agents/workspace.ts` against real on-disk directories under an isolated `OPENCLAW_HOME`, reproducing the nested-workspace seeding path a subagent run hits. Branch cut from current `origin/main`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: created an established workspace at `<parent>/.openclaw/workspace-state.json`; created a nested project directory `<parent>/github/my-project` containing `.git/` and `README.md` (no marker of its own); invoked `ensureAgentWorkspace({ dir: nested, ensureBootstrapFiles: true })`; then listed the nested directory. Ran it on this branch (with the fix) and again with `src/agents/workspace.ts` reverted to `origin/main` (without the fix).
- Before evidence (without the fix, on `origin/main`): the nested project directory is littered with generated bootstrap files —
  ```
  nested dir BEFORE ensureAgentWorkspace: .git README.md
  nested dir AFTER  ensureAgentWorkspace: .git .openclaw AGENTS.md HEARTBEAT.md IDENTITY.md README.md SOUL.md TOOLS.md USER.md
  ```
- Evidence after fix: the same real run, on this branch, leaves the nested project directory exactly as it was —
  ```
  nested dir BEFORE ensureAgentWorkspace: .git README.md
  nested dir AFTER  ensureAgentWorkspace: .git README.md
  ```
- Observed result after fix: the nested project directory is left untouched — `ensureAgentWorkspace` no longer writes `AGENTS.md`, `SOUL.md`, `TOOLS.md`, `IDENTITY.md`, `USER.md`, `HEARTBEAT.md`, or a nested `.openclaw/` into it. A brand-new (empty) nested directory, and a nested directory that owns its own marker, both still seed/repair, so freshly created and established secondary agents are unaffected.
- What was not tested: a live Telegram/macOS end-to-end subagent spawn through a model. The reproduction above drives the exact production `ensureAgentWorkspace` filesystem path the subagent flow uses; the reporter's original root-level symptom is separately addressed by the existing cwd/workspace split, so this targets the remaining source-reproducible nested case.

## Automated checks (supplemental)

- `src/agents/workspace.test.ts`: 49/49, including three new regression tests covering the ancestor-marker boundary (inherited content skipped; brand-new nested still seeded; own-marker nested still repaired).
- `src/agents/subagent-spawn.workspace.test.ts`, `spawned-context.test.ts`, `bootstrap-files.test.ts`, `attempt.cwd-split.test.ts`, `attempt.spawn-workspace.sessions-spawn.test.ts`: all green.
- `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint`, `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:core:test`: clean.

Fixes #83593

target.title: fix(xai): respect ssrfPolicy and request.allowPrivateNetwork in image_generate
target.body:
## Summary


- **Problem**: `extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.ts` hardcodes `resolveAllowPrivateNetwork: () => false`, blocking xAI image generation when the user configures a private-network gateway (e.g., `http://10.0.0.10:8090`). The SSRF guard fires regardless of `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` or `models.providers.xai.request.allowPrivateNetwork`.
- **Solution**: Replace the hardcoded `false` with config-aware logic that reads `browser.ssrfPolicy` (via `isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled`) and `models.providers.xai.request.allowPrivateNetwork`, matching the pattern already used by the OpenAI image provider (#63095).
- **What changed**: One file — `extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.ts` — +1 import, +1 logic line.
- **What did NOT change**: Other providers with the same hardcoded pattern (e.g., `extensions/deepinfra/`), xAI chat runtime, xAI auth flow, or any core SSRF logic. Scoped strictly to xAI image generation per issue scope.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [x] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related to #84627 (scoped to xAI image generation only; other providers with same pattern not fixed)
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

The xAI image provider's `resolveAllowPrivateNetwork` was hardcoded to `false`, ignoring both `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` and `models.providers.xai.request.allowPrivateNetwork` config. Users with private-network xAI gateways (multi-tenant proxies, internal endpoints) are blocked from using xAI image generation even when they've explicitly opted in via config. The OpenAI equivalent was fixed in #63095; this applies the same fix to xAI.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed**: xAI `image_generate` blocked by SSRF when using a private-network base URL, despite user config opting in.
- **Real environment tested**: Unit tests (8 tests, all passing) + code review. The tests cover default deny, browser.ssrfPolicy opt-in, and provider request.allowPrivateNetwork opt-in paths. The fix follows the identical pattern proven in production since #63095 (OpenAI).
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  ```bash
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.test.ts --run
  ```
- **Evidence after fix**:
  ```console
  $ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.test.ts --run
  [test] starting test/vitest/vitest.extension-providers.config.ts

   RUN  v4.1.7

   ✓ |extension-providers| extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.test.ts (8 tests) 315ms

   Test Files  1 passed (1)
        Tests  8 passed (8)
     Start at  09:54:27
     Duration  1.70s

  3 new SSRF tests:
  ✓ defaults allowPrivateNetwork to false when no SSRF opt-in is configured
  ✓ allows private network when browser.ssrfPolicy opts in
  ✓ allows private network when xai provider request.allowPrivateNetwork is set
  ```
  Unit test coverage showing the three SSRF decision paths:
  ```typescript
  // Test 1: Default deny - no config → allowPrivateNetwork: false
  expect(httpParams?.allowPrivateNetwork).toBe(false);

  // Test 2: browser.ssrfPolicy opt-in → isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled returns true → allowPrivateNetwork: true
  isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabledMock.mockReturnValueOnce(true);
  expect(httpParams?.allowPrivateNetwork).toBe(true);

  // Test 3: xai provider request.allowPrivateNetwork → even when isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled false → true
  isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabledMock.mockReturnValueOnce(false);
  expect(httpParams?.allowPrivateNetwork).toBe(true);
  ```
  The code diff (same pattern as OpenAI #63095):
  ```console
  $ git diff origin/main...HEAD -- extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.ts
  diff --git a/extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.ts b/extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.ts
  index b1d7c05ef..970db3528 100644
  --- a/extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.ts
  +++ b/extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.ts
  @@ -12,6 +12,7 @@ import {
     normalizeOptionalLowercaseString,
     normalizeOptionalString,
   } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/string-coerce-runtime";
  +import { isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/ssrf-runtime";
   import { XAI_BASE_URL, XAI_DEFAULT_IMAGE_MODEL, XAI_IMAGE_MODELS } from "./model-definitions.js";

   const DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS = 600_000;
  @@ -106,7 +107,9 @@ export function buildXaiImageGenerationProvider(): ImageGenerationProvider {
       },
       defaultBaseUrl: XAI_BASE_URL,
       resolveBaseUrl: ({ req }) => resolveXaiImageBaseUrl(req),
  -    resolveAllowPrivateNetwork: () => false,
  +    resolveAllowPrivateNetwork: ({ req }) =>
  +      isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled(req.cfg?.browser?.ssrfPolicy) ||
  +      Boolean(req.cfg?.models?.providers?.xai?.request?.allowPrivateNetwork),
       defaultTimeoutMs: DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS,
       buildGenerateRequest: ({ req, inputImages, model, count }) => ({
         kind: "json",
  ```
  The `isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled` function (shared, tested in `src/plugin-sdk/ssrf-policy.test.ts`):
  ```console
  $ node -e "
  const f = require('./dist/plugin-sdk/ssrf-runtime.js').isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled;
  console.log('Default:', f(undefined));
  console.log('Opted in:', f({dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: true}));
  "
  Default: false
  Opted in: true
  ```
- **Observed result after fix**: All 8 tests pass. The three SSRF-specific tests verify:
  1. Default (no config) → `allowPrivateNetwork: false` (default deny preserved) ✓
  2. `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: true` → `isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled` → `allowPrivateNetwork: true` ✓
  3. `models.providers.xai.request.allowPrivateNetwork: true` → `allowPrivateNetwork: true` (independent opt-in path) ✓
  The fix matches the identical pattern proven in the OpenAI provider (#63095). `isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled` is the same function already used by OpenAI and covered by shared unit tests.
- **What was not tested**: Live E2E with a real private-network xAI gateway (requires xAI API key + private gateway access — unavailable in this environment). Other providers with the same hardcoded pattern (`extensions/deepinfra/`). xAI chat runtime (unrelated).

## Root Cause

`extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.ts:109` — `resolveAllowPrivateNetwork: () => false` was copied from the initial provider scaffold and never updated to respect user config.

## Regression Test Plan

Added three SSRF opt-in tests in `extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.test.ts`:
1. Default deny (no opt-in config → `allowPrivateNetwork: false`)
2. browser.ssrfPolicy opt-in → `allowPrivateNetwork: true`
3. xai provider request.allowPrivateNetwork opt-in → `allowPrivateNetwork: true`

All 8 tests pass. The existing `src/plugin-sdk/ssrf-policy.test.ts` suite covers `isPrivateNetworkOptInEnabled` itself.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

Users who have configured `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: true` or `models.providers.xai.request.allowPrivateNetwork: true` will no longer get SSRF-blocked when using xAI image generation with a private-network base URL.

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No — opt-in only, same as OpenAI already allows
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No — only changes the SSRF guard decision
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Repro + Verification

### Environment

- Branch: `fix/xai-ssrf-allow-private-network-84627`
- Base: `origin/main` (44e6caff5)

### Steps

1. Configure `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: true` in `openclaw.json`
2. Set `models.providers.xai.baseUrl` to a private-network address
3. Run `image_generate` with xAI model

### Expected

Image generation succeeds; no SSRF block.

### Actual (before fix)

```
[security] blocked URL fetch (url-fetch) targetOrigin=http://10.0.0.10:8090
  reason=Blocked hostname or private/internal/special-use IP address
[image-generation] candidate failed: xai/grok-imagine-image: Blocked hostname...
```

## Verification

- [ ] Failing test/log before + passing after
- [ ] Trace/log snippets
- [ ] Screenshot/recording
- [ ] Perf numbers (if relevant)

## Human Verification

- **Verified scenarios**: Three SSRF opt-in tests (default deny, browser policy, provider config) + 5 pre-existing tests = 8 total passing. Both config paths independently tested.
- **Edge cases checked**: Default deny when neither config is set; browser policy opt-in alone; provider config opt-in alone when browser policy returns false.
- **What you did NOT verify**: Live E2E with real xAI private gateway (requires xAI API key + private gateway). Other providers with identical hardcoded pattern (`extensions/deepinfra/`).

## Review Conversations

- [ ] I replied to or resolved every bot review conversation I addressed in this PR.
- [ ] I left unresolved only the conversations that still need reviewer or maintainer judgment.

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — default behavior unchanged (both config checks return `false` when unset)
- [x] Config/env changes? No — no new config keys
- [x] Migration needed? No

## AI Assistance

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes
- **AI prompts / session excerpts**: "fix #84627 — xAI image_generate blocked by SSRF — resolveAllowPrivateNetwork hardcoded to false in extensions/xai/image-generation-provider.ts"

## Risks and Mitigations

None. This is a strict superset of the existing logic — when neither config is set, it returns `false` (same as the hardcoded default). The same pattern has been proven in production since #63095 (OpenAI).

---

target.title: fix(browser): keep CDP discovery on the configured host
target.body:
Related: #100819
Follow-up to #100986

AI-assisted: Codex implemented and reviewed this change; the maintainer verified the trust-boundary decisions and live proof.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where browser users with permissive or multi-host navigation policy could let CDP discovery follow a returned debugger WebSocket to a host other than the configured browser endpoint. The same page policy also leaked into persistent Playwright tab creation and permission grants, while strict local-relay configurations could block legitimate loopback control.

## Why This Change Was Made

CDP control now gets a dedicated exact-host policy after preserving the existing remote `hostnameAllowlist` gate. Configured local relays keep their loopback control exception, discovered endpoints cannot claim one, and Playwright plus permission routes use the control policy only for CDP connections while retaining the page policy for navigation.

## User Impact

Browser automation keeps working for managed and extension loopback profiles under strict navigation rules. Explicitly allowed remote CDP profiles still work, excluded remote hosts remain blocked, and discovery cannot pivot control traffic or CDP URL credentials to another navigation-allowed host.

## Evidence

- Fresh `autoreview` against current `main`: clean after all actionable findings were fixed.
- Targeted `oxfmt --check` across all 12 changed files: pass.
- Added strict, permissive, wildcard, trailing-dot, extension-loopback, discovered-endpoint, persistent Playwright, and permission-route regressions.
- Exact rebased head `5a33fe8d345b493dc0345bcc898192e53901e316`, sanitized AWS Crabbox `cbx_72d43a28c47b` (`m7i.xlarge`, public network, no Tailscale or instance role).
- `pnpm test extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.internal.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/chrome.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/chrome.internal.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-session.connections.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-session.termination-cdp-ssrf.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.remote-profile-tab-ops.playwright.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/permissions.test.ts`: 9 files, 236 tests passed.
- Live run `run_087175c3f407`: real Chrome 150, Gateway, and `openai/gpt-5.4` agent. CDP open/list worked under a restrictive navigation allowlist; direct and agent navigation to `openai.com` were policy-blocked; the existing tab remained on `example.com`; agent summary recorded 3 tool calls including browser with zero failures.

target.title: feat(context-engine): report compaction successors as typed session targets
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Context engines that own compaction report their post-compaction successor session to the host through `CompactResult.result.sessionFile` — a raw file-path string. A bare path cannot say which agent/session it belongs to or what storage mode backs it, so every consumer re-infers identity from a path, and the contract cannot describe non-file-backed sessions.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a typed successor contract: `CompactResult.result.sessionTarget` (`{ kind: "file", agentId?, sessionId, sessionKey?, sessionFile }`) makes storage mode explicit and carries precise identity. The delegate populates it; host consumers (`adoptCompactionTranscript`, `runOwnsCompactionAfterHook`, queued-compaction rotation detection) read target-first with the raw-field fallback centralized in one helper (`resolveCompactionSuccessorTranscript`). This matches the direction main already took for runtime params in `run-session-target.ts`.

`CompactResult` is a shipped plugin-SDK surface (exported via `plugin-sdk/index.ts`, present in release tag v2026.6.11, documented in `docs/concepts/context-engine.md` for third-party engine authors), so `sessionFile` stays populated and is marked `@deprecated` naming that shipped contract, with removal planned once typed targets are the only successor contract.

## User Impact

None for existing plugins — `sessionFile` keeps working unchanged. Engine authors get a typed, documented successor contract; docs updated accordingly.

## Evidence

- Consumer map verified: all in-scope `CompactResult.sessionFile` readers migrated (`run.ts` adoption paths, `compact.queued.ts` rotation detection, delegate producer); the four look-alike readers of the runtime `EmbeddedAgentCompactResult` type confirmed out of scope at each site.
- `context-engine.test.ts` updated bridge test + 2 new tests; 206/206 tests pass across the five suites exercising compaction adoption paths.
- Plugin SDK API baseline regenerated via the sanctioned `plugin-sdk:api:gen` for the intentional surface addition; `pnpm build` green (SDK export checks pass).
- oxfmt/oxlint clean; structured review (codex/gpt-5.5) clean, zero findings.

target.title: fix(msteams): add graphMediaFallback so group-chat file attachments reach the agent
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Files attached to Microsoft Teams **group chat** messages never reach the agent, even with all recommended Graph Application permissions granted (#89594). Teams strips the `<attachment id="…">` tags from the message HTML it delivers to bots in group chats, so `extractMSTeamsHtmlAttachmentIds` returns an empty list and the existing Graph media fallback in `resolveMSTeamsInboundMedia` never fires. The Graph copy of the same message retains both the tag and the full `reference` attachment (SharePoint `contentUrl` + name), so the already-implemented `downloadMSTeamsGraphMedia` path works fine once it is allowed to run — the gate is the only blocker.

Verified discrepancy on a live tenant (same message, `19:…@thread.v2` group chat, plugin 2026.6.11):

- Bot Framework activity: one `text/html` attachment, plugin diagnostics `{'htmlAttachments': 1, 'attachmentTags': 0, 'attachmentIds': []}`
- Graph `GET /chats/{chatId}/messages/{messageId}`: body HTML contains `<attachment id="…"></attachment>` and `attachments: [{ contentType: "reference", contentUrl: "https://…sharepoint.com/…/file.pdf", name: "file.pdf" }]`

## Why This Change Was Made

The gate exists for a good reason — mention-only group messages also arrive as `text/html` attachments, and keying on contentType alone caused spurious Graph lookups and 404 diagnostics (#58617). So instead of relaxing the gate unconditionally, this adds an explicit opt-in:

`channels.msteams.graphMediaFallback` (default: `false`) — for non-personal conversations that carried a `text/html` attachment and yielded no media, attempt the Graph message fetch even when no `<attachment id>` tags were extracted.

- Default `false`: behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged, including the #58617 protection (covered by existing tests, which still pass unmodified).
- Enabled: costs one Graph message lookup per group/channel message that yields no downloadable media (including mention-only messages) — the trade-off is documented in `docs/channels/msteams.md`. Requires `Chat.Read.All` (+ `ChannelMessage.Read.All` for channels) and `Files.Read.All`/`Sites.Read.All` Application permissions with admin consent.
- Personal (Bot Framework `a:`/`8:orgid:`) chats are unaffected — they keep the Bot Framework v3 attachments path.

## User Impact

Operators whose agents live in Teams group chats can enable one config flag and file attachments (PDFs, docs, images uploaded as files) become readable by the agent. Everyone else sees no change.

## Evidence

- Live validation: an equivalent gate relaxation applied to a production 2026.6.11 install (macOS, single-tenant bot) — a PDF attached to a group-chat message was fetched via the Graph reference path (`downloaded attachments {'count': 1}`) and the agent answered questions about its content. Before the change, the same message produced `graph fallback never attempted` (extraction all-zero) and the agent saw no file.
- `pnpm vitest run extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/inbound-media.test.ts` — 15 passed (12 existing unmodified + 3 new: enabled-flag group fetch, default-off unchanged, personal-chat exclusion)
- `pnpm test:extension msteams` — 70 files, 998 tests passed
- `pnpm check` — clean
- `pnpm test:contracts:channels` — 34 passed

Fixes #89594

target.title: fix(agents): preserve preflight overflow token counts into recovery budgeting
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a rendered prompt overflows preflight token checks, the overflow token counts observed during preflight were dropped before recovery ran. Compaction engines then compacted against a stale/underestimated size instead of the prompt OpenClaw actually rendered, and context-engine assembly was not budgeted against the compaction reserve plus rendered prompt pressure before the precheck.

## Why This Change Was Made

Recovery decisions should use the best token evidence available at the moment of failure:

- A `buildPreflightRecoveryBudgetSnapshot` helper captures estimated prompt tokens, pre-reserve prompt budget, and observed overflow tokens into every token-pressure-driven `preflightRecovery` assignment.
- Overflow recovery falls back `observedOverflowTokens → preflightEstimatedPromptTokens → minimally-over-budget`, and logs `preflightEstimatedTokens=` for diagnosis.
- Context-engine assembly budgets `tokenBudget` as context budget minus compaction reserve minus rendered prompt pressure, passing the reserve as `maxOutputTokens`.

The aggregate tool-result char-pressure recovery site keeps no snapshot deliberately — no token estimate exists in that scope; the optional fields plus the fallback chain cover it.

## User Impact

Agents recovering from prompt overflow compact against realistic sizes, reducing repeated overflow/compaction loops on long sessions. No config or API changes; the new `preflightRecovery` fields are optional.

## Evidence

- New synthetic-overflow test in `run.overflow-compaction.test.ts` and a context-engine assembly budget test in `run/attempt.spawn-workspace.context-engine.test.ts`; 120 tests pass across the two touched test files.
- tsgo core + core-test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on all six touched files.

target.title: fix(google-vertex): add Google Vertex AI onboarding wizard, fix ADC auth, add provider docs
target.body: ## Summary **What problem does this PR solve?** The `google-vertex` provider does not work end-to-end for developers using Application Default Credentials (ADC). The auth gate requires a credentials file on disk, rejecting metadata server ADC (GCE/GKE/Cloud Run) before the transport layer can run. The onboarding wizard has no auth flow for google-vertex, doesn't register models in the provider config, doesn't prompt for GCP project/location, has no model catalog, and has no dedicated documentation. **Why does this matter now?** Multiple open issues document this problem (#56253, #79595, #85864, #79837, #11413). We reproduced the issue on a fresh install: a new OpenClaw install requires numerous manual undocumented steps and manual edits to JSON config to get a working `google-vertex` setup. Users on GCE/GKE with valid GCP credentials consistently hit "No API key found" because the auth gate only accepts file-based ADC. **What is the intended outcome?** A developer picks "Google Vertex AI" in the onboarding wizard, confirms their auto-detected GCP project, and sends a message. Three steps without manual config editing. **What is intentionally out of scope?** - Changes to the `google` (AI Studio) or `google-gemini-cli` providers **What does success look like?** `openclaw onboard --auth-choice google-vertex-adc` on a GCE VM (or any machine with ADC configured) produces a working setup with zero manual config editing. **What should reviewers focus on?** - The new `"env-vars-with-marker"` auth evidence type (`src/secrets/provider-env-vars.ts`, `src/plugins/manifest.ts`, `src/agents/model-auth-env.ts`) - The relaxed auth gate in `src/llm/env-api-keys.ts` (accepts project OR credentials file OR credentials env var, no longer requires all three) - The `configPatch` model registration approach in `extensions/google/provider-contract-api.ts` (workaround for `applyPrimaryModel` not persisting `models.providers` through the wizard config serialization) - The `gcp-vertex-credentials` marker profile stored during onboarding for auth detection All changes were reviewed and tested by the author on a fresh VM. ## Linked context **Which issue does this close?** Related #56253, #85864, #79595, #79837, #11413 **Which issues, PRs, or discussions are related?** Related #49191, #50053, #52476, #48910, #77643, #55572, #53566, #9729 See also #83971 (merged, fixed transport-layer ADC but not the upstream auth gate) **Was this requested by a maintainer or owner?** No. Reproduced independently on a GCE VM based on multiple open issues reporting the same auth failure. ## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs) - **Behavior or issue addressed:** google-vertex provider fails with "No API key found" on GCE VMs using metadata server ADC. Onboarding wizard provides no auth flow, no model catalog, and no documentation path for google-vertex users. - **Real environment tested:** Fresh VM (e2-standard-4, Debian 12, Cloud Platform access scope), OpenClaw built from this branch. - **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** ```bash pnpm openclaw uninstall --all --yes pnpm openclaw onboard --auth-choice google-vertex-adc # Confirmed auto-detected project # Accepted "global" location # Kept default model (google-vertex/gemini-flash-latest) # Hatched in Terminal, sent "Wake up, my friend!" ``` - **Evidence after fix:** - **Observed result after fix:** Gemini responded successfully via Vertex AI with ADC from the GCE metadata server. No auth warnings during onboarding. Model catalog populated in "Browse all models." Project auto-detected. target.title: fix(usage): preserve provider-billed zero totals
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Follow-up to #97047 after the direct DeepSeek V4 zero-cost regression was fixed on `main`.

The remaining accounting gap is that `usage.cost.total: 0` is ambiguous in persisted transcripts:

- it can be a fabricated placeholder zero from a transport/catalog path, which should be recomputed or treated as missing when pricing is known/unknown; or
- it can be an authoritative provider-billed total from a provider billing endpoint, including a legitimate free/zero-cost route.

OpenRouter is the concrete provider-billed case: its generation metadata endpoint returns `total_cost`, and that value is the provider's billing total. When `total_cost` is `0`, core usage aggregation should preserve it only when the transcript carries explicit provenance proving that the zero came from provider billing.

## Why This Change Was Made

The earlier follow-up approach was rejected because it guessed from provider/model ids and treated every known-priced all-zero row as authoritative. This version follows the maintainer guidance instead:

- no DeepSeek/OpenRouter model ids are hard-coded into core usage accounting;
- OpenRouter, as the provider owner, marks generation-metadata totals as provider-billed;
- core aggregation uses a generic provenance signal rather than provider-specific policy;
- rows without provenance keep the current `main` behavior, so suspicious known-priced zero totals still get recomputed.

## What Changed

- Add `usage.cost.totalOrigin?: "provider-billed" | "estimated"` to the usage/cost type contract.
- When OpenRouter generation metadata lookup succeeds, set:
  - `usage.cost.total = data.total_cost`
  - `usage.cost.totalOrigin = "provider-billed"`
- Teach session usage-cost scanning to preserve recorded zero totals when `totalOrigin` is `provider-billed`.
- Keep the existing protection for provider-reconciled zero totals with nonzero cost components.
- Keep existing recomputation/missing-cost behavior for unproven all-zero known-priced/unknown-priced rows.
- Bump the durable usage-cost cache version from 6 to 7 because recognized cost-total provenance changes cached total semantics.

## Evidence

Regression coverage added/updated:

- `extensions/openrouter/index.test.ts`
  - nonzero OpenRouter generation metadata cost is marked `provider-billed`
  - zero OpenRouter generation metadata cost is marked `provider-billed`
  - failed/oversized generation metadata lookup keeps the streamed estimate and does not set provider-billed provenance
- `src/infra/session-cost-usage.test.ts`
  - provider-billed all-zero cost total with known pricing remains zero in summary, durable cache, and session logs
  - known-priced transcript rows without provider-billed provenance still recompute from catalog pricing
  - version-6 durable cache entries are stale under the new provenance-aware semantics

Local targeted validation on the pushed head:

- `git diff --check -- src/agents/usage.ts packages/llm-core/src/types.ts src/infra/session-cost-usage.types.ts src/infra/session-cost-usage.ts src/infra/session-cost-usage.test.ts extensions/openrouter/stream.ts extensions/openrouter/index.test.ts`
- `CI=1 NO_COLOR=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/infra/session-cost-usage.test.ts extensions/openrouter/index.test.ts`
  - `src/infra/session-cost-usage.test.ts`: 66 passed
  - `extensions/openrouter/index.test.ts`: 46 passed

## Relationship to Closed PRs

This supersedes the closed #97134 and #101163 follow-up attempts. The closed PRs tried to resolve the conflict by scoping behavior from core. This PR instead adds the explicit provenance contract requested in review.

## Conflict Resolution

The branch is based on current `openclaw/openclaw@3accc99b43` and has no merge conflict with `main`.

## Risk

Low-to-moderate behavior risk, limited to cost accounting for transcript rows with `usage.cost.total: 0`.

Expected behavior after this change:

- Provider-billed zero total with explicit `totalOrigin: "provider-billed"`: preserved as authoritative zero.
- Known-priced placeholder zero without provenance: recomputed from catalog pricing.
- Unknown/all-zero pricing with nonzero tokens and no provenance: still reported as missing cost.
- Positive recorded provider costs: preserved by existing behavior.

No workflow, dependency, lockfile, secret, or release artifact changes.

target.title: fix(clawhub): bound archive download bodies
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

ClawHub package, ClawPack, skill, resolver, and GitHub-source archive paths all omitted a practical body limit; the shared reader defaulted to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. A hostile or broken registry could therefore grow gateway memory until the process failed.

Supersedes #100999 because its conflicting branch was converged into a clean maintainer rewrite. Contributor authorship is preserved in the squashed commit.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Give the shared ClawHub byte reader the same 256 MiB archive ceiling already used by marketplace downloads.
- Preserve the explicit 256 KiB skill-card limit.
- Reject trustworthy identity `Content-Length` declarations before buffering while measuring encoded responses from their decoded stream bytes.
- Exercise every archive entry point, declared-oversize cancellation, and encoded-body behavior while retaining the shared reader's streamed overflow guard.

## User Impact

ClawHub installs now fail with a bounded, resource-specific error instead of allowing oversized archive responses to exhaust gateway memory. Normal archives and skill cards keep their existing behavior.

target.title: fix(ports): ignore malformed lsof listener pids
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a listener-diagnostics bug where malformed `lsof -F` `p` records could still attach subsequent `n` address lines to a listener entry with no valid PID. That could surface bogus busy-port diagnostics from corrupted or partial `lsof` output instead of reporting only real listening processes.

## Why This Change Was Made

`src/infra/ports-inspect.ts` now accepts only positive parsed PIDs from `lsof` process records and skips listener address rows that are not attached to a valid process. This keeps the diagnostics path aligned with the stricter PID validation already used in nearby port-inspection code.

## User Impact

Gateway port diagnostics now ignore malformed `lsof` process rows instead of showing phantom listeners with missing or invalid process identity. Valid listener output is unchanged.

## Evidence

### Unit Tests
Fresh focused test runs on commit 16369d50 (after the latest manual `main` merge into this branch):

```bash
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/ports.test.ts src/cli/program.force.test.ts
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.infra.config.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  16 passed (16)
   Start at  09:35:28
   Duration  1.17s (transform 700ms, setup 604ms, import 29ms, tests 301ms, environment 0ms)

[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.cli.config.ts

 RUN  v4.1.8 /home/0668000995/10288592/git-hub/test/openclaw

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  22 passed (22)
   Start at  09:35:35
   Duration  1.17s (transform 678ms, setup 491ms, import 192ms, tests 161ms, environment 0ms)

[test] passed 2 Vitest shards in 19.99s
```

Coverage called out by Codex is present on the current branch head:
- `src/infra/ports.test.ts` keeps the repeated-listener dedupe test
- `src/infra/ports.test.ts` rejects malformed diagnostics tokens like `p111abc`
- `src/cli/program.force.test.ts` rejects malformed force-free tokens like `p111abc`

### Real Behavior Proof (for ClawSweeper/Codex)

The earlier review correctly flagged that mocked Vitest output alone was not enough. Below is a fresh real run from the current branch head, executing the production parser helper directly with `tsx` and no test harness mocks.

```bash
$ node --import tsx ./tmp-pid-proof.mjs
=== Real production code execution (no mocks) ===
Legacy behavior:  Number.parseInt("111abc", 10) = 111
Fixed behavior:   parseStrictPositiveInteger("111abc") = undefined

Legacy behavior would have accepted pid 111 from a corrupted lsof "p" record.
Fixed behavior correctly returns undefined so the record is dropped.
```

The code path now used by diagnostics is `src/infra/ports-inspect.ts:53-56`:

```typescript
if (line.startsWith("p")) {
  const pid = parseStrictPositiveInteger(line.slice(1));
  processFields = pid !== undefined ? { pid } : {};
}
```

The sibling force-free parser is hardened the same way in `src/cli/ports.ts:148-153`, so both lsof `p`-field surfaces now reject digit-prefixed garbage instead of truncating it to a valid PID.

**Result:** a malformed token like `p111abc` no longer becomes pid `111` on either path. Diagnostics drop the listener record, and `gateway run --force` no longer risks signaling the wrong process because of `parseInt` truncation.

**Current coverage summary:**
- Valid PIDs (positive integers) → accepted
- Empty/missing pid record (`p`) → skipped
- Garbage token (`pabc`) → skipped
- Trailing-garbage token (`p111abc`) → skipped on both diagnostics and force-free paths
- Repeated identical listener records for one process/address → deduplicated
- Address rows without a valid PID context → ignored

The built-in grep tool owned a piped ripgrep child but did not handle stdout or stderr stream failures. Node treats an unhandled `error` event as process-fatal, and readline removes its input-error listener when the interface closes, so a pipe failure could crash the agent runtime or escape after cleanup.

The implementation mirrors the landed find-tool invariant without adding a new shared abstraction.

Duplicate proof scaffolding and the root changelog edit were removed. Test kill state is modeled without mutating Node's readonly child-process property.

## User Impact

Grep tool calls fail with a contextual stdout/stderr error instead of crashing the Gateway, hanging, or returning incomplete matches.

target.title: security fix(gateway): defend pre-auth device-signature verify against CPU DoS
target.body:
Closes #77979

## Summary

- Pre-auth WS handshakes that include a `device` block ran `crypto.createPublicKey` plus a v3-then-v2 `crypto.verify` per request, gated only by frame-size limits. An unauthenticated remote attacker could pin a single Gateway core: PoC against a real running gateway hits **~510 forged handshakes/s/IP**, degrading legit handshake p50 by **48.7×** (1.16 ms → 56.6 ms) and p99 by **94.7×**.
- Fix is layered: schema cap on `device.publicKey` (1024) and `device.signature` (256); shape pre-check on `verifyDeviceSignature` / `deriveDeviceIdFromPublicKey` / `normalizeDevicePublicKeyBase64Url` rejecting inputs that cannot decode to a 32-byte raw key or 64-byte signature; new `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_SCOPE_DEVICE_SIGNATURE` bucket gating the verify per IP. The browser-origin rate limiter is always constructed (`server.impl.ts:424`), so the gate fires for browser-origin clients even when no `gateway.auth.rateLimit` is configured. For non-browser-origin clients, the gate fires when the operator configures a rate limiter (the typical production case).
- Loopback exemption is preserved so legit local CLI sessions are never throttled; the gate fires through the non-loopback-exempt limiter for remote and browser-origin clients, which is the production threat path.

## Reproduction

The PoC (`scripts/poc-preauth-flood-ws.mjs`) opens N concurrent WS connections, each completing the connect-challenge handshake with a real Ed25519 PEM public key and a random 64-byte signature. The gateway reaches the verify path (server-issued nonce echoed back, `device.id` matches `sha256(rawPublicKey)`) and runs `createPublicKey` + v3 `verify` + v2 `verify` per request. A separate measurement client probes time-to-first-event in parallel.

Against a vulnerable gateway:

```
pnpm gateway:watch                                    # in another terminal

node scripts/poc-preauth-flood-ws.mjs \
     --gateway ws://127.0.0.1:18789 \
     --attackers 32 \
     --legit-iters 30 \
     --duration-ms 3000
```

Observed:

```
baseline:     n=30 p50=1.16ms  p90=1.80ms  p99=2.04ms
under-attack: n=30 p50=56.58ms p90=64.24ms p99=193.36ms
attacker totals: connections=1531  rate=510/s   (one IP, one node process)
legit handshake p50 ratio (under-attack / baseline): 48.69x
legit handshake p99 ratio: 94.73x
```

To validate the fix end-to-end without exposing a dev gateway to the LAN, the in-process integration test runs the same forged-handshake sequence against a real `withGatewayServer` instance configured with `rateLimit.maxAttempts: 1, exemptLoopback: true`:

```
pnpm test src/gateway/server.preauth-signature-rate-limit.test.ts
```

The test asserts:
1. The first N forged signatures fail with `error.details.reason === "device-signature"` (the verify ran).
2. The (N+1)th attempt fails with `error.details.reason === "device-signature-rate-limited"` and `retryAfterMs > 0` — the gate short-circuited before any crypto.

Reverting the `recordFailure` line in the rate-limit gate makes both tests fail with `expected 'device-signature' to be 'device-signature-rate-limited'`.

## Test plan

- [x] `src/gateway/server.preauth-signature-rate-limit.test.ts` — new in-process WS integration test (2 cases). Both fail when the fix is disabled.
- [x] `src/infra/device-identity.test.ts` — new shape pre-check tests: oversized PEM, oversized non-PEM, signature-shaped input rejected as public key, public-key-shaped input rejected as signature, all without invoking crypto.
- [x] `src/gateway/protocol/connect-device-bounds.test.ts` — new schema-cap tests: `validateConnectParams` rejects oversized `device.publicKey` and `device.signature`; accepts them at the documented bounds.
- [x] Existing `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/handshake-auth-helpers.test.ts` — 27/27 pass, no regression.
- [x] Live PoC reproduction confirms the 50× p50 / 95× p99 degradation pre-fix.

## Verification

- Targeted `pnpm test` of the four affected files: 41/41 pass.
- Build: dist contains the new rate-limit gate (`grep AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_SCOPE_DEVICE_SIGNATURE` on the bundle).
- Type errors observed during local `pnpm tsgo` are pre-existing and unrelated (`pi-embedded-runner.*` AgentMessage casts and missing `web-tree-sitter` dep).

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed**: pre-auth `device` blocks ran `crypto.createPublicKey` plus a v3-then-v2 `crypto.verify` per request with no per-IP cap. An unauthenticated attacker could pin a Gateway core (~510 forged handshakes/s/IP, 48.7× p50 / 94.7× p99 degradation against legitimate handshakes per the network-level PoC numbers above). The fix layers three defenses: ajv schema caps reject oversized `device.publicKey` and `device.signature` before any handler runs; `isPlausibleDevicePublicKeyInput` / `isPlausibleDeviceSignatureInput` shape pre-checks reject inputs that cannot decode to a 32-byte raw key or 64-byte signature without invoking crypto; and `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_SCOPE_DEVICE_SIGNATURE` gates the verify per IP, so once the bucket is exhausted no `createPublicKey` or `verify` runs.
- **Real environment tested**: local Node v22.22.2 runtime against the real patched modules from this branch (`security/preauth-signature-rate-limit` HEAD `6233fc0e60`). No vitest, no mocks. The reproducer imports `validateConnectParams` from the patched `protocol/index.ts`, the cap constants and `isPlausibleDevice*` helpers from `infra/device-identity.ts`, and `createAuthRateLimiter` from `gateway/auth-rate-limit.ts`, then exercises each layer against representative attacker payloads.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**: a node runtime tsx reproducer at https://gist.github.com/fede-kamel/974f456b4269b7242e1c91b9dc46c178 runs three layers — schema caps against oversized `device.publicKey`/`device.signature` (including a 60 KB representative attacker payload), shape pre-checks against malformed inputs that decode to wrong-length raw bytes, and the `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_SCOPE_DEVICE_SIGNATURE` bucket fired against a single attacker IP. Run as `node --import tsx <local-copy>.mts` from a worktree on this branch.
- **Evidence after fix**: live terminal output captured from the node runtime against the patched modules:

```
Pre-auth device-signature CPU-DoS proof (PR 77492)
Imports real patched validateConnectParams + isPlausibleDevice* + AuthRateLimiter
from security/preauth-signature-rate-limit worktree.

MAX_DEVICE_PUBLIC_KEY_INPUT_CHARS = 1024
MAX_DEVICE_SIGNATURE_INPUT_CHARS  = 256
ED25519_RAW_PUBLIC_KEY_BYTES      = 32
ED25519_SIGNATURE_BYTES           = 64

=== Layer 1: schema-level rejection of oversized device.publicKey / device.signature ===

case                                                          | result | took
--------------------------------------------------------------|--------|------
valid: device.publicKey real PEM (113 chars)                  | PASS   | 4.494ms
reject: device.publicKey at 1025 chars (cap+1)                | REJECT | 0.515ms
reject: device.publicKey at 60KB (representative attacker payload)| REJECT | 4.246ms
reject: device.signature at 257 chars (cap+1)                 | REJECT | 0.077ms

=== Layer 2: shape pre-check on device-identity helpers (no crypto) ===

case                                                          | result | took
--------------------------------------------------------------|--------|------
valid: real raw 32-byte base64url public key                  | PASS   | 0.486ms
valid: real PEM public key                                    | PASS   | 0.039ms
reject: random 100-byte base64                                | REJECT | 0.629ms
reject: oversized publicKey (cap+1)                           | REJECT | 0.053ms
reject: empty publicKey                                       | REJECT | 0.048ms
valid: real 64-byte base64url signature                       | PASS   | 0.101ms
reject: random 32-byte signature input                        | REJECT | 0.118ms
reject: oversized signature (cap+1)                           | REJECT | 0.035ms
reject: 60KB signature                                        | REJECT | 0.044ms

=== Layer 3: rate-limit gate AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_SCOPE_DEVICE_SIGNATURE ===

attempt | rateLimited | remaining/retryAfterMs | crypto entered?
--------|-------------|------------------------|------------------
    1   | false       | remaining=3            | would enter
    2   | false       | remaining=2            | would enter
    3   | false       | remaining=1            | would enter
    4   | true        | retryAfterMs=60000     | skipped
    5   | true        | retryAfterMs=59999     | skipped
    6   | true        | retryAfterMs=59999     | skipped
    7   | true        | retryAfterMs=59999     | skipped
    8   | true        | retryAfterMs=59999     | skipped

=== Layer 3b: cost comparison — skipped vs entered ===

crypto entered 5000 times: 214.3ms (avg 0.043ms/op)
gate-blocked  5000 times: 62.6ms (avg 0.013ms/op)
amplification factor under attack: 3.4x
```

- **Observed result after fix**: every legitimate input validated `PASS` and every cap+1 / 60 KB / wrong-length / wrong-shape attacker input validated `REJECT` across both schema (Layer 1) and shape pre-check (Layer 2). The rate-limit gate (Layer 3) blocked attempts 4 through 8 from a single attacker IP after the configured `maxAttempts: 3`, never reaching `createPublicKey`/`verify`. Layer 3b measured the per-op cost of the full Ed25519 verify path (0.043 ms/op) versus the gate-blocked path (0.013 ms/op) — a 3.4× per-op CPU saving on every attempt past the threshold, which compounds against the 510/s/IP attacker rate observed in the network-level PoC.
- **What was not tested**: the WS upgrade and connect-challenge wire protocol are not driven by this reproducer; that integration shape is covered by `server.preauth-signature-rate-limit.test.ts` (in-process WS server) and by the live `scripts/poc-preauth-flood-ws.mjs` PoC against a running `pnpm gateway:watch`. Concurrent multi-IP attacker behavior was not measured in this reproducer; the gate is per-IP and isolation matches the existing device-token bucket.

## Notes for reviewer

- This branch is also flagged `triage: dirty-candidate` because the diff touches schema, device-identity helpers, and the WS message handler. The three layers are intentionally tightly coupled — the schema cap is a cheap fast-reject, the shape pre-check covers in-spec but malformed inputs that pass the schema, and the rate-limit gate covers attackers presenting in-shape Ed25519 keypairs (their own). Splitting the layers would either leave one layer behind a partial defense or duplicate the fix surface across PRs. Happy to split if reviewers prefer one layer per PR.
- The `recordFailure` is intentionally pessimistic before crypto runs — an attacker with their own keypair producing valid self-signatures should still consume the bucket. `reset` only fires after `resolveConnectAuthDecision` confirms the full handshake is authorized.

target.title: fix(macos): prevent hatch and web chat from timing out on slow first replies
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where macOS onboarding/web chat could make a slow first assistant reply look stuck or prematurely timed out when the selected model takes longer than the old client-side budget. This matters for first-run hatch/chat paths with slower models such as OpenAI 5.5, where the user expects the assistant to keep working after they describe its purpose.

The mismatch was that the macOS WebChat path needed a longer assistant-run budget and a completion observation path, while the request/ACK deadline should still fail quickly when the gateway is unreachable.

## Why This Change Was Made

This separates the short request/ACK deadline from the actual WebChat assistant run budget. The shared `GatewayConnection.chatSend` default stays request-sized so other macOS callers such as Talk Mode keep their existing timeout policy, while `MacGatewayChatTransport.sendMessage` explicitly opts WebChat/hatch into a five-minute `timeoutMs` run budget.

The shared chat UI now reads its pending/completion budget from the active transport. The default transport budget remains 120 seconds, while macOS WebChat overrides it to five minutes and waits for completion through the existing Gateway `agent.wait` surface before refreshing history. The change does not alter gateway protocol shape, auth, provider routing, model selection, session storage, schema, migrations, or delivery channels.

## User Impact

macOS users hatching or chatting with a newly configured assistant now get a realistic wait window and a production completion observation path for slow first replies instead of a premature timeout or stuck-looking state while the assistant run may still be active or recently completed.

The intended behavior is that macOS WebChat/hatch keeps gateway ACK failures prompt while giving only the WebChat assistant run, UI pending state, and completion refresh path the first-run-sized five-minute window.

## Evidence

- Current-head freshness: PR head `70ce9e068ac79a4fd092425806c45903101e06ce`.
- Current-head packaged macOS app metadata:
  ```text

  OpenClawBuildTimestamp=2026-07-06T19:11:13Z

- Current-head real app process and real Chat window:

  gateway: current checkout dev gateway, port 19001, matching local gateway token

  ```
- Exact packaged-app proof steps after this patch:
  ```bash

    ALLOW_ADHOC_SIGNING=1 SIGN_IDENTITY="-" ./scripts/package-mac-app.sh

  node openclaw.mjs --dev gateway
  dist/OpenClaw.app/Contents/MacOS/OpenClaw --chat --attach-only
  ```
- Slow prompt sent through the real `OpenClaw Chat` input box, not through `gateway call chat.send`:
  ```text
  Please run this exact terminal command using the terminal and do not reply until it finishes: sleep 90; echo OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE. After it finishes, reply exactly OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE.
  ```
- Visual/OCR proof from the same real packaged `OpenClaw Chat` window:
  ```text
  PROOF WebChat send, real window after UI Return key:
  OpenClaw Chat
  Please run this exact terminal command using the terminal and do not reply until it finishes: sleep 90; echo OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE. After it finishes, reply exactly OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE.
  • Writing
  Message...
  • Gateway connected

  PROOF WebChat still pending after 35 seconds, same real window at 2026-07-06T19:55:00Z:
  OpenClaw Chat
  Please run this exact terminal command using the terminal and do not reply until it finishes: sleep 90; echo OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE. After it finishes, reply exactly OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE.
  • Writing
  Message...
  • Gateway connected

  PROOF WebChat completion observed later, same real window at 2026-07-06T19:56:45Z:
  OpenClaw Chat
  Please run this exact terminal command using the terminal and do not reply until it finishes: sleep 90; echo OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE. After it finishes, reply exactly OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE.
  OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE
  Message...
  • Gateway connected
  ```
- Observed result after fix: the current-head packaged macOS WebChat app stayed in the visible `Writing` pending state more than 35 seconds after a real UI send, did not show a timeout, and later displayed `OPENCLAW_UI_70CE9E0_SLOW_REPLY_DONE` with the pending indicator gone.
- What was not tested: no video recording; the proof above is terminal/visual text copied from the real packaged macOS app window plus process and app metadata.
- Regression tests and local checks:
  ```text
  swift test --filter 'OpenClawIPCTests.GatewayConnectionControlTests/`agent wait sends run id and timeout`()|OpenClawIPCTests.GatewayConnectionControlTests/`mac chat transport exposes first-run sized pending timeout`()|OpenClawIPCTests.GatewayConnectionControlTests/`mac chat transport opts into first-run sized agent timeout`()'
  ✔ Test run with 3 tests in 1 suite passed after 0.031 seconds.

  swift test --filter 'OpenClawKitTests.ChatViewModelTests/`completion wait uses transport opted in timeout`()'
  ✔ Test run with 1 test in 1 suite passed after 0.024 seconds.

  node --import tsx scripts/native-app-i18n.ts check
  native-app-i18n: entries=2752 changed=false
  ```

## Regression Test Plan

- Coverage level: Swift unit tests plus macOS terminal behavior proof.
- Target test files: `apps/macos/Tests/OpenClawIPCTests/GatewayConnectionControlTests.swift`, `apps/shared/OpenClawKit/Tests/OpenClawKitTests/ChatViewModelTests.swift`.
- Scenario locked in: macOS WebChat sends `timeoutMs == 300_000`, completion waits use the transport-scoped budget, pending runs survive past 30 seconds, and pending state clears after completion.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: the tests cover the two changed seams directly: macOS transport timeout selection and shared chat pending/completion state.

## Root Cause

- Root cause: the macOS WebChat send path used one short timeout value for both request/ACK delivery and the assistant run budget, so a slow first reply could look timed out or stuck even while the gateway run was still active.
- Missing detection / guardrail: there was no regression coverage proving macOS WebChat opts into a first-run-sized assistant budget while preserving the shorter shared/default request timeout.

target.title: fix(cron): expose flat cron job fields and normalize malformed tool args
target.body:
Related: #3569 
Related: #64721

## What Problem This Solves

`src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts` exposes a TypeBox schema to models in Openclaw where almost everything is `Type.Optional`. However the contract is enforced downstream in `normalize.ts` and `persisted-shape.ts` meaning fields that looked optional become required depending on which `kind` was chosen. The code says at ln 54–55:

> "Spell out job/patch properties for model-facing schema; runtime validation still happens in
> normalizeCronJob* to avoid nested union schemas."

In practice this means that openclaw gets no useful feedback from mistakes. Typical failures seen in testing: emitting the `job` argument as a truncated string instead of an object; supplying a top-level `mode` (valid only for the `wake` action); choosing a schedule kind without its required field (e.g. `kind: "cron"` with no `expr`, or omitting `payload.kind`); and passing `toolsAllow`/`fallbacks` as a scalar string instead of an array. Rejection gives generic error messages such as "jobId required" and "job required" with no field-level detail, so the openclaw doesn't have sufficient information to fix the problem. 

## Why This Change Was Made

I mostly use local Gemma 4 26b Q5 which became  completely unable to amend my cron jobs following upgrade to v6 Openclaw. However this is not simply a local LLM issue as Codex also had difficulties. Codex's greater reasoning power allowed for workrounds but with clearer schema these workarounds and iterative fixes wouldn't be needed.

I see that #3569 reported the same issues and the report was later closed through PR #10776. But #10776 did not address the TypeBox schema. @gerroon reported that fails still happen on their Qwen-30b-Instruct after the fix.

Also #64721 reports the same kind of problem: `payload.model`, `payload.timeoutSeconds`,
`payload.contextTokens`, and `maxSpendUsd` are accepted at runtime but the schema rejects
them as unexpected properties.

 Fix could be with a discriminated union, making the model reason about nested conditional types. However my concern is that lower-reasoning local LLMs will not manage this reasoning adequately.

Therefore instead the patch adds a flat top-level field set as an alternative to the nested `job` object:

| Field           | Type    | Notes                                          |
| --------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `name`          | string  | job name                                       |
| `enabled`       | boolean |                                                |
| `sessionTarget` | string  | `main \| isolated \| current \| session:<id>`  |
| `at`            | string  | ISO-8601, one-shot                             |
| `everyMs`       | integer | recurring interval in ms                       |
| `expr`          | string  | cron expression                                |
| `tz`            | string  | IANA timezone for `expr`                       |
| `message`       | string  | agentTurn prompt — implies `agentTurn` payload |
| `anchorMs`      | integer | start anchor for `everyMs` schedules           |
| `model`         | string  | agentTurn model override                       |
| `fallbacks`     | string[]| agentTurn fallback models                      |
| `toolsAllow`    | string[]| agentTurn allowed tool ids                     |
| `thinking`      | string  | agentTurn thinking override                    |
| `timeoutSeconds`| number  | agentTurn timeout override                     |

The canonicalizer (`cron-tool-canonicalize.ts`) infers `schedule.kind` and `payload.kind` from whichever fields are present, so the model never has to deal with the nested union. Also
descriptions for `text` (implies `systemEvent`) and `mode` (wake only, not delivery mode)
have been tightened up.

The implementation now also normalises scalar toolsAllow / fallbacks into arrays and reconstructs job / patch from recoverable flat fields when the request is clearly a cron add/update call.  This deals with an issue found in testing where openclaw incorrectly tries toolsAllow as a scalar string, or emits a malformed non-object job / patch alongside flat fields.  

## User Impact

Upstream already recovers flat params at runtime: 
`recoverCronObjectFromFlatParams` in `cron-tool-canonicalize.ts` (with
`CRON_FLAT_PAYLOAD_KEYS` / `CRON_FLAT_SCHEDULE_KEYS`)

The patch simply exposes in the model-facing schema what the runtime already accepts but doesn't show. Note the nested `job` form still works also.  There is no negative user impact to the fix.

## Evidence

Tested on OpenClaw gateway version 2026.6.10
OS: Linux Mint 22.3 (Zena)
Kernel: Linux 6.17.0-23-generic (x86_64)
LLMs used for testing: Local Gemma 4 26b Q5 (llama.cpp); openai/gpt-5.4
Tests designed and run by: Claude (Anthropic Claude Opus 4.8); OpenAI Codex (gpt-5.4)

Focused validation on `fix/cron-tool-schema-fix` (`~/code/openclaw-main`) currently passes for the actual patch surface:

- `corepack pnpm test src/agents/tools/cron-tool.schema.test.ts src/agents/tools/cron-tool.test.ts`
  - schema shard: `20 passed`
  - agents shard: `135 passed`

These tests cover:

- flat-field exposure in the model-facing cron schema
- canonicalization of malformed flat `toolsAllow` / `fallbacks`
- synthesis of `job` / `patch` from recoverable flat arguments
- the drift guard that ensures any advertised flat field is still recoverable by the canonicalizer

Earlier branch testing also included:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/cron-tool.schema.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/cron-tool.test.ts`
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test`

Live installed testing on patched OpenClaw 2026.6.10 also succeeded in creating disposable cron jobs through the flat-field interface, confirming the path works in a real installed gateway and not only in unit tests.

This four-file branch is green on the patch-local validation that actually exercises the cron-tool
change. The remaining PR-guide blockers are upstream baseline failures outside this patch scope.

Current upstream-baseline validation also shows:

- latest `origin/main` still fails `corepack pnpm deps:shrinkwrap:check` with
  `npm-shrinkwrap.json is stale. Run pnpm deps:shrinkwrap:generate.`
- clean `origin/main` is also currently red in unrelated test areas, including
  `src/gateway/server-methods/agent.test.ts` and `src/media-understanding/image.test.ts`
  (reported for completeness only)

So the branch is green for the cron-tool patch itself, while the remaining `check` / full-suite
`test` reds are upstream, pre-existing, and unrelated to this four-file change. codex review --base origin/main stated the patch appears to correctly expose the flat cron fields and normalize them before validation without introducing a concrete regression in the touched surfaces.

target.title: fix(message-tool): parse inline [[...]] button JSON from model text output
target.body:
## Summary

- Some models (e.g. Gemini) output button definitions like `[[{"text":"Label","callback_data":"data"}]]` as raw text in the message body instead of using the interactive blocks parameter.
- Add `extractInlineButtons()` helper that scans text for double-bracket-wrapped JSON button arrays using bracket-aware + brace-aware scanning.
- Supports both single-row `[{...}]` and multi-row `[[{...}],[{...}]]` formats, as well as bare object `{...}` and comma-separated `{...},{...}` formats that Gemini sometimes emits.
- Integrate extraction into **two delivery paths**:
  1. `createMessageTool().execute` (message-tool text sanitization) — for when models use the message tool
  2. `copyPayloadWithSanitizedText` in `agent-runner-payloads.ts` — for automatic final replies that bypass the message tool (the path reported in the linked issue)
- Extracted buttons are converted to `MessagePresentation.buttons` blocks (or `interactive` blocks in the message-tool path) and injected into the payload, with the raw `[[...]]` marker text removed from the visible output.

## Parser fix (addressing review P1 findings)

**Original bug:** `findClosingDoubleBracket` tracked only `[`/`]` depth (not `{`/`}` brace depth), causing JSON object-internal `]` to be misidentified as closing `]]` markers for the `[[{"text":"X","callback_data":"Y"}]]` format described in the PR body and the linked issue.

**Fix:** Now tracks both `bracketDepth` and `braceDepth`. When `braceDepth > 0`, `]` inside a JSON object context is skipped, preventing misidentification. Also fixed `innerText` slice range: `closeIdx` points to the second `]` of `]]`, so `innerText` must use `slice(openIdx+2, closeIdx-1)` (not `closeIdx`).

**Additional:** `parseButtonRows` now handles bare object `{...}`, comma-separated objects `{...},{...}`, and comma-separated arrays `[{...}],[{...}]` — formats Gemini sometimes emits without a proper JSON array wrapper.

## Path coverage fix (addressing review P1 finding)

**Original gap:** `extractInlineButtons` was only called inside `createMessageTool().execute`. Current group prompts tell the model not to use the message tool for the same group (groups.ts:255: "For ordinary text, do not use the message tool to send to this same group; just reply normally"), so the reported final-reply path bypassed the extraction entirely.

**Fix:** Added extraction in `copyPayloadWithSanitizedText` (agent-runner-payloads.ts), which runs on all automatic reply payloads during text sanitization. Extracted buttons are injected as `MessagePresentationButtonsBlock` entries into the payload `presentation.blocks` field, ensuring both delivery paths are covered.

## Verification

- 17 unit test cases covering: single button, multi-button row, triple bracket, multi-row array-of-arrays, Gemini format with spaces (issue #41495 exact reproducer), comma-separated objects/arrays, bare object format, TTS directive safety, mixed tts + buttons, multiple blocks, empty input, invalid JSON, arrays of strings, non-button brackets, style, whitespace cleanup, issue #41495 end-to-end.
- All 17 tests pass.
- Existing `[[tts:voice]]` and `[[reply_to_current]]` directive parsing is unaffected.

Closes #41495

target.title: feat(gateway): add allowedOriginPatterns for constrained loopback port wildcards
target.body:
Closes #98383

## What Problem This Solves

Remote WebView-hosted node clients (e.g. phone companion apps using Even Hub or similar frameworks) connect to the Gateway WebSocket with dynamically-assigned local origins like `http://127.0.0.1:<random-port>`. The current `gateway.controlUi.allowedOrigins` only supports exact origins or the global `["*"]` wildcard, forcing users to choose between two inadequate options:

- **Per-port allowlisting**: requires updating the config on every app restart, impractical for end users
- **`["*"]` wildcard**: disables browser origin checks entirely, a significant security regression

## Why This Change Was Made

Added `gateway.controlUi.allowedOriginPatterns` — a constrained pattern list that accepts only `scheme://loopback-host:*` patterns. The implementation touches three layers with clearly separated responsibilities:

**1. Zod schema (config load time — fail-close)**

Each pattern must pass six checks: valid format (`scheme://host:*`), explicit protocol (`http:` or `https:`), port-level `*` wildcard only, no host wildcards, and hostname in the loopback literal set (`127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, `[::1]`). Illegal patterns prevent service startup — no silent downgrades.

**2. Runtime matching (`checkBrowserOrigin`)**

A new `origin-pattern` matching branch is inserted between the existing allowlist check and the local-client fallback. This preserves exact-match priority (`allowedOrigins` wins over patterns) and all existing fallback paths (`host-header-fallback`, `private-same-origin`, `local-loopback`) remain untouched. The runtime also includes a redundant `isLoopbackHost` guard as defense-in-depth against non-loopback patterns that bypassed schema validation.

**3. Startup config validation**

- `server-runtime-config.ts`: the non-loopback bind check now accepts `allowedOriginPatterns` as valid origin configuration — users deploying on a public bind with only patterns configured will not be blocked
- `gateway-control-ui-origins.ts`: `hasConfiguredControlUiAllowedOrigins` recognizes patterns so the auto-seed logic does not overwrite explicit user configuration

**4. Codex review follow-up**

- `schema.help.ts`: aligned `allowedOriginPatterns` help text style with `allowedOrigins`, added "Patterns are evaluated alongside allowedOrigins; either match is sufficient for WebSocket access" to clarify the union relationship
- `origin-check.test.ts`: added two HTTP trusted-proxy path tests confirming `allowedOriginPatterns` is correctly propagated through `resolveHttpBrowserOriginPolicy` → `authorizeTrustedProxyBrowserOrigin` → `checkBrowserOrigin`
- `audit-gateway-config.ts`: updated security audit to recognize `allowedOriginPatterns` as valid origin configuration, suppressing false `allowed_origins_required` findings
- `zod-schema.ts`: added `.describe()` metadata for `allowedOriginPatterns`
- `schema.help.ts`: updated `allowedOrigins` help text to reference `allowedOriginPatterns` as a safer alternative for dynamic loopback port clients
- `docs/gateway/configuration-reference.md` and `docs/gateway/troubleshooting.md`: added `allowedOriginPatterns` to public docs and origin-error remediation guidance
- `docs/gateway/security/index.md`: added `allowedOriginPatterns` to Gateway security notes
- `docs/gateway/trusted-proxy-auth.md`: updated trusted-proxy guidance (4 references) to include `allowedOriginPatterns`
- `docs/gateway/security/audit-checks.md`: updated audit-check table description and config column
- `legacy-config-migrations.runtime.gateway.ts`: passed `allowedOriginPatterns` through doctor migration so `openclaw doctor --fix` does not seed exact origins over a patterns-only config
- `ui/src/i18n/locales/en.ts`: added Control UI origin-error guidance referencing `allowedOriginPatterns` for dynamic loopback port scenarios

**Design constraints preserved across the stack:**

- No regular expressions beyond the fixed format parser — no ReDoS surface
- No host wildcards, no protocol wildcards, no implicit IP equivalence (`localhost` ≠ `127.0.0.1`)
- No DNS queries — loopback detection is pure string literal matching
- Hostname normalization between `parseOrigin` and `parseOriginPattern` is consistent: trailing-dot stripping applied in both directions
- Non-goals: client/role scoping, exact-port matching, DNS-resolution-based detection, pre-parsed pattern caching (current per-call cost is ~500ns, negligible relative to WebSocket handshake)

## User Impact

Users hosting Gateway on a public (non-loopback) address can now configure:

```json
{
  "gateway": {
    "controlUi": {
      "allowedOriginPatterns": ["http://127.0.0.1:*"]
    }
  }
}
```

This allows WebSocket connections from any remote WebView running on `http://127.0.0.1:<any-port>` without resorting to `["*"]`. The full loopback family is supported (`127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, `[::1]`, both `http:` and `https:` protocols).

**No existing behavior is changed** — all of the following continue to work identically:

- `allowedOrigins` exact matches (higher priority than patterns)
- `allowedOrigins: ["*"]` global wildcard (unchanged)
- `isLocalClient` loopback fallback (unchanged)
- `host-header-fallback` (unchanged)
- `private-same-origin` for LAN/tailscale hosts (unchanged)
- Non-loopback deployments with explicit `allowedOrigins` (unchanged)

Users currently on `["*"]` for WebView support can migrate to `["http://127.0.0.1:*"]` and regain origin-check protection while maintaining the same operational behavior.

**Compatibility note:** `allowedOriginPatterns` is an optional new field that
defaults to an empty array. Existing configurations are fully backward-compatible;
no data migration or manual upgrade is required for existing deployments. The
Zod schema rejects illegal patterns at load time (fail-close), so once a valid
config is accepted, it will remain valid across future versions.

## Evidence

**Runtime verification** (`npx tsx` against real source, no mocks, no test framework):

```

─── A: Zod Schema allowedOriginPatterns (11/11) ───
  ✅ A1: http://127.0.0.1:* accepted

  ✅ A8: bare * rejected
  ✅ A9: ftp protocol rejected
  ✅ A10: empty patterns array accepted (no regression)
  ✅ A11: allowedOrigins + allowedOriginPatterns coexist

─── B: checkBrowserOrigin runtime matching (15/15) ───
  ✅ B1: http://127.0.0.1:40313 matches pattern [CORE ISSUE SCENARIO]
  ✅ B2: http://localhost:5173 matches http://localhost:*

```
